overview.title: Regression templates and ConvNets in review
overview.main_topic: The end of the densely connected network recap (multilabel classification, regression) and the start of the ConvNet recap: what convolution does, why it is data efficient, and a typical SeparableConv2D image classifier.
overview.central_idea: The last layer and the loss are dictated by the task: regression ends with a Dense layer with no activation trained with MSE. ConvNets apply the same local transformation at every location, which makes them translation invariant and data efficient, and they alternate convolutions with pooling before collapsing to a vector for a Dense head.
overview.importance: This is a cheat sheet. The code templates on this page and the next ones are the patterns you will reach for most often when starting a new project, and the paragraphs condense chapters 4, 8 and 9 into a few sentences.
learning_objectives: Choose the right final layer and loss for multilabel classification and for regression.
Explain why a regression output layer has no activation and why MSE is the default loss.
State what a convolution layer computes and why that makes it translation invariant and data efficient.
Pick Conv1D, Conv2D or Conv3D (or SeparableConv2D) depending on the dimensionality of the data.
Explain the role of max pooling and of the final Flatten or global pooling step in a ConvNet.

The Keras Functional API (keras.Input, calling layers on tensors, keras.Model), p.219.

summary:
This page is part of section 20.1.6, a compact review of the network architectures used throughout the book. It finishes the **densely connected networks** recap from p.625 and starts the **ConvNets** recap.

**End of the multilabel template.** The first code block is the tail of the multilabel classification example started on p.625: a hidden `Dense(32, relu)` layer, then an output `Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid")`, compiled with `binary_crossentropy`. Each output unit is an independent yes/no probability, which is what k-hot targets need.

**Regression.** To predict a vector of continuous values, end with a `Dense` layer whose number of units equals the number of values to predict (often one, like a house price) and **no activation**, so the output can take any real value. Several regression losses exist; the most common is `mean_squared_error` (`"mse"`). The template is a two-hidden-layer MLP (`Dense(32, relu)` twice) compiled with `rmsprop`.

**ConvNets.** Convolution layers look at **spatially local patterns** by applying the *same* transformation to every patch of the input. The result is **translation invariant** (a pattern learned in one place is recognized anywhere), which makes convolution **data efficient and modular**. The idea works in any number of dimensions: `Conv1D` for sequences, `Conv2D` for images, `Conv3D` for volumes. **Depthwise separable convolutions** (`SeparableConv2D`) are a leaner, more efficient drop-in alternative.

A ConvNet stacks convolution and **max-pooling** layers. Pooling downsamples the feature maps, which keeps their size reasonable as the number of channels grows and lets later convolutions "see" a larger part of the input. At the end, a `Flatten` or **global pooling** layer turns the feature maps into a vector, and `Dense` layers do the classification or regression. The page closes with the first half of a typical image classifier built from `SeparableConv2D` layers (32, 64, pool, 64, 128 filters), which continues on p.627.

paragraphs.excerpt: To perform regression toward a vector of continuous values, end your stack
paragraphs.what_it_says: For regression, the network should end with a Dense layer that has one unit per value to predict (often just one, such as a house price) and no activation. Several losses are possible, and mean_squared_error (MSE) is the most common.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The output layer of a regression model must be able to produce any real number. An activation such as sigmoid would squash outputs into (0, 1) and relu would forbid negative values, so the last layer is left linear: $\hat y = W h + b$. MSE then penalizes the squared distance between prediction and target. The 'vector of continuous values' wording means the same template handles multi-output regression: `num_values` output units, one per target.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Getting the output activation wrong is one of the most common beginner mistakes in regression. A model with a sigmoid output on unscaled prices simply cannot fit the data, whatever you do with the rest of the network.
paragraphs.technical_idea: With a linear output and MSE loss, training is equivalent to maximum-likelihood estimation under a Gaussian noise assumption (beyond the book). MAE is the main alternative and is less sensitive to outliers; chapter 4 monitored MAE as a metric while training with MSE (p.152).

terminology.meaning: Predicting a continuous value (or vector of values) rather than a discrete class.
A linear (identity) output: the layer returns W·h + b unchanged, so any real value is reachable.
Mean squared error: the average of (prediction - target)^2 over samples and outputs.

connections: p.150: the housing-price regression example in chapter 4 used exactly this kind of output layer and MSE loss.
p.625: the classification templates that precede this one differ only in the last layer's units/activation and the loss.

paragraphs.excerpt: Convolution layers look at spatially local patterns by applying the same geometric
paragraphs.what_it_says: Convolution layers apply the same transformation to every local patch of an input tensor. This gives translation-invariant representations, which makes convolution data efficient and modular. The idea works for 1D sequences, 2D images and 3D volumes, via Conv1D, Conv2D and Conv3D. Depthwise separable convolutions such as SeparableConv2D are a leaner, more efficient alternative.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A convolution kernel is a small set of weights (say 3×3×C_in for each output channel) that slides across the input; the same weights are used everywhere (weight sharing). Two consequences follow. First, a pattern learned at one location is detected at every location, so the model does not need separate training examples of a cat's ear in each corner: that is the data efficiency. Second, because each layer only looks locally and the next layer combines those local features, ConvNets build hierarchies of increasingly abstract patterns: that is the modularity. Strictly, a convolution is translation *equivariant* (shifting the input shifts the feature map); invariance of the final prediction comes from pooling and global pooling on top.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the architecture prior that made deep learning work for vision. Picking a layer whose built-in assumptions match the structure of the data (here: patterns are local and can appear anywhere) is one of the best ways to improve generalization, as the book argued in chapter 5 (p.179).
paragraphs.technical_idea: A depthwise separable convolution first applies one spatial filter per input channel (depthwise) and then mixes channels with a 1×1 convolution (pointwise). For a 3×3 kernel with C_in inputs and C_out outputs, the weight count drops from 9·C_in·C_out to 9·C_in + C_in·C_out.

terminology.meaning: A small local window of the input (for example 3×3 pixels across all channels) that one application of the kernel looks at.
The property that a pattern is recognized regardless of where it appears in the input.
A factorized convolution: per-channel spatial filtering followed by a 1×1 channel-mixing convolution.

connections: p.259: chapter 8 introduced the two key properties of ConvNets: translation-invariant patterns and spatial hierarchies.
p.386: Conv1D was used on temperature timeseries in chapter 13.
p.302: SeparableConv2D was introduced as a drop-in replacement for Conv2D in chapter 9.

paragraphs.excerpt: ConvNets, or convolutional networks, consist of stacks of convolution and max-pooling layers.
paragraphs.what_it_says: A ConvNet stacks convolution and max-pooling layers. Pooling downsamples the data, which keeps feature maps at a reasonable size as the number of features grows and lets later convolutions see a larger spatial extent of the input. ConvNets usually end with a Flatten or global pooling layer that turns the feature maps into vectors, followed by Dense layers for classification or regression. The paragraph then introduces a typical categorical image classifier built with SeparableConv2D layers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There are two reasons to downsample. The first is cost: channels typically grow from 32 to 128 or more while you go deeper, so if the spatial size did not shrink, the activations would become enormous. The second is receptive field: a 3×3 kernel after two 2×2 poolings covers a 12×12 region of the original image, so the top layers can respond to object-level patterns. The final step collapses the spatial axes. Flatten keeps every position (many parameters in the next Dense layer); global average pooling keeps one number per channel, which is cheaper and less prone to overfitting.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This conv → pool → ... → global pool → Dense pattern is the skeleton of nearly every image classifier in the book (chapter 8, 9, the Xception-like model on p.304), so recognizing it lets you read and design such models quickly.
paragraphs.technical_idea: In the example, the convolutions use the default `padding="valid"`, so each 3×3 layer also trims 2 pixels from height and width; most of the downsampling still comes from MaxPooling2D(2), which halves both spatial dimensions.

terminology.meaning: Downsampling that keeps the maximum value of each channel in each window (here 2×2, stride 2).
Pooling over the whole spatial extent, reducing a (h, w, c) feature map to a (c,) vector.
The (height, width, channels) output of a convolution layer; each channel records where one learned pattern is present.

connections: p.263: chapter 8 explained the max-pooling operation and why downsampling is needed.
p.265: the book argued max pooling works better than strides or average pooling for intermediate downsampling.
p.269: the cats-vs-dogs model ended with GlobalAveragePooling2D before the Dense output.

concepts.name: Regression output layer
concepts.definition: A final Dense layer with one unit per predicted value and no activation, usually trained with mean squared error.
concepts.intuition: You want a number line, not a probability: the last layer must be free to output any real value.
concepts.technical: outputs = Dense(num_values)(x); loss='mse'. The absence of activation means the output is an affine function of the last hidden representation.
concepts.significance: This is the standard head for any continuous-target problem, from house prices to bounding-box coordinates.
concepts.example: Predicting a house price: Dense(1) output, MSE loss, MAE monitored as a readable metric.
concepts.misconception: Adding relu to guarantee positive prices seems harmless, but it creates dead outputs whose gradient is zero whenever the pre-activation is negative.

concepts.name: Mean squared error
concepts.definition: The average of the squared differences between predictions and targets; the most common regression loss.
concepts.intuition: Large errors count disproportionately: being off by 10 costs 100 times more than being off by 1.
concepts.technical: $\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (\hat y_i - y_i)^2$. In Keras: loss='mse' or 'mean_squared_error'.
concepts.significance: Smooth and easy to optimize with gradient descent; sensitive to outliers.
concepts.misconception: MSE is not in the units of the target; its square root (RMSE) or MAE is easier to interpret.

concepts.name: Convolution layer
concepts.definition: A layer that applies the same small learned filter to every local patch of its input, producing a feature map.
concepts.intuition: A stencil you slide over the picture: wherever the stencil matches, the output lights up.
concepts.technical: Conv2D(filters, kernel_size) learns a kernel of shape (k, k, C_in, filters); weights are shared across positions. Conv1D and Conv3D do the same over 1 or 3 spatial axes.
concepts.significance: Weight sharing gives translation invariance and huge parameter savings, making vision models data efficient.
concepts.example: A 3×3 edge detector learned once detects edges anywhere in a 180×180 image.
concepts.misconception: Convolution alone is equivariant, not invariant: the feature map shifts with the input. Invariance of the final decision comes from pooling.

concepts.name: Translation invariance
concepts.definition: The property that a learned pattern is recognized wherever it appears in the input.
concepts.intuition: A face is a face whether it is in the top-left or bottom-right of the photo.
concepts.technical: Arises from weight sharing in convolutions (equivariance) combined with pooling (invariance to small shifts) and global pooling (invariance to position).
concepts.significance: The visual world is fundamentally translation invariant, so models with this prior need fewer training samples.
concepts.example: A Dense network trained on MNIST would have to relearn a stroke at every position; a ConvNet learns it once.
concepts.misconception: ConvNets are not invariant to rotation or scale by construction; those must be learned (for example via data augmentation).

concepts.name: Depthwise separable convolution
concepts.definition: A convolution factored into a per-channel spatial convolution followed by a 1×1 pointwise convolution that mixes channels.
concepts.intuition: First look for spatial shapes in each channel separately, then decide how to combine channels.
concepts.technical: Parameters: k·k·C_in + C_in·C_out (+ biases), versus k·k·C_in·C_out for Conv2D. Assumes spatial correlations and cross-channel correlations can be learned separately.
concepts.significance: Smaller, faster, and in the book's experience often slightly more accurate than regular convolution; the basis of Xception.
concepts.example: 3×3, 64→128 channels: Conv2D needs 73,728 weights, SeparableConv2D needs 576 + 8,192 = 8,768.
concepts.misconception: It is not always better: on the very first layer with 3 input channels, the savings are small and the factorization assumption is weaker.

concepts.name: Max pooling and global pooling
concepts.definition: Downsampling operations: max pooling keeps the maximum in each small window; global pooling reduces each whole channel to one number.
concepts.intuition: Ask 'was this feature present somewhere in this region?' rather than 'exactly where?'
concepts.technical: MaxPooling2D(2) halves height and width. GlobalAveragePooling2D maps (h, w, c) to (c,).
concepts.significance: Keeps feature maps small and grows the receptive field of later layers; global pooling connects the convolutional base to the Dense head.
concepts.example: A (176, 176, 64) feature map becomes (88, 88, 64) after MaxPooling2D(2).
concepts.misconception: Pooling has no trainable weights; it does not 'learn' to downsample.

code.title: End of the multilabel classification template (begun on p.625)
code.original_code:
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(num_classes, activation="sigmoid")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="binary_crossentropy")
code.what_it_does: Finishes a multilabel classifier: a hidden ReLU layer, then one sigmoid unit per class, compiled with binary crossentropy so that each class is treated as an independent yes/no decision.

line_explanations.explanation: Second hidden Dense layer (the inputs and the first hidden layer are on p.625).
One output unit per class with sigmoid: each unit outputs an independent probability in (0, 1), so several classes can be 'on' at once.
Functional API: build a Model from the symbolic input and output tensors.
binary_crossentropy is applied per output unit and averaged; targets must be k-hot vectors of 0s and 1s.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a feature vector of length num_input_features (defined on p.625). Output: a vector of num_classes independent probabilities.
code.algorithm: Two-layer MLP with a per-class logistic output.
code.theory_link: Sigmoid + binary crossentropy per unit is the maximum-likelihood setup for independent Bernoulli labels; softmax would wrongly force the class probabilities to sum to 1.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.role: Number of possible labels; equals the length of the k-hot target vector.

parameters.name: optimizer="rmsprop"
parameters.role: The book's default optimizer for these small templates.

pitfalls: Using softmax here would make the labels compete; one confident label would suppress the others.
Predictions must be thresholded (for example at 0.5) per class to get a set of labels.

code.title: Regression template
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(num_input_features,))
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.Dense(32, activation="relu")(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(num_values)(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="mse")
code.what_it_does: Builds a small MLP that maps a feature vector to num_values continuous outputs, trained with mean squared error.

line_explanations.explanation: Symbolic input: a batch of vectors with num_input_features entries each (the batch dimension is implicit).
Two hidden Dense layers of 32 ReLU units: the learnable nonlinear feature extractor.
Output layer with num_values units and no activation, so outputs are unbounded real numbers.
Wrap inputs and outputs into a Model.
Compile with RMSprop and MSE loss. In practice you would also add metrics=["mae"] to read the error in target units, as in chapter 4.

code.inputs_outputs: Input shape (batch, num_input_features); output shape (batch, num_values).
code.algorithm: Gradient-descent fit of a nonlinear function minimizing squared error.
code.theory_link: Linear output + MSE is the standard regression head; chapter 4 (p.152) used the same structure for house prices.

parameters.name: num_input_features
parameters.role: Number of input features per sample.

parameters.name: num_values
parameters.role: Number of continuous targets to predict (often 1).

parameters.name: loss="mse"
parameters.role: Mean squared error, the most common regression loss.

pitfalls: Normalize input features (and often targets) first; features on very different scales make training slow and unstable.
On small datasets, evaluate with K-fold validation rather than a single split, as in chapter 4 (p.153).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: same template with a readable metric
model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="mse", metrics=["mae"])
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=100, batch_size=16, validation_split=0.2)

code.title: SeparableConv2D image classifier, first half (continues on p.627)
code.original_code:
inputs = keras.Input(shape=(height, width, channels))
x = layers.SeparableConv2D(32, 3, activation="relu")(inputs)
x = layers.SeparableConv2D(64, 3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.MaxPooling2D(2)(x)
x = layers.SeparableConv2D(64, 3, activation="relu")(x)
x = layers.SeparableConv2D(128, 3, activation="relu")(x)
code.what_it_does: Starts the convolutional base of an image classifier: two separable convolution layers, a 2×2 max pooling, then two more separable convolutions with more filters.

line_explanations.explanation: Image input in channels-last format: (height, width, channels), for example (180, 180, 3).
Two 3×3 depthwise separable convolutions with 32 and 64 filters and ReLU. Default padding is 'valid', so each trims 2 pixels from height and width.
Two more separable convolutions; the number of filters grows (64 → 128) as resolution shrinks, the typical ConvNet pattern.

code.inputs_outputs: Input (batch, height, width, channels). After line 6, with a 180×180×3 input: (batch, 84, 84, 128).
code.algorithm: Stacked conv-conv-pool blocks, building a spatial hierarchy of features.
code.theory_link: Implements the 'stacks of convolution and max-pooling layers' described in e08, with the leaner separable convolutions from e07.

parameters.name: filters (32, 64, 64, 128)
parameters.role: Number of output channels (learned patterns) per layer.

parameters.name: kernel_size=3
parameters.role: Each filter looks at 3×3 spatial windows.

parameters.name: MaxPooling2D(2)
parameters.role: Pool size 2 with stride 2: halves height and width.

pitfalls: The first separable convolution on a 3-channel image saves little compared with Conv2D; some architectures use a regular Conv2D as the first layer.
The code is incomplete on this page; the classification head is on p.627.

deeper.title: Why separable convolutions are 'leaner': counting parameters
deeper.body:
Take the fourth layer of the example: 3×3 kernel, 64 input channels, 128 output channels.

- **Conv2D**: $3\cdot3\cdot64\cdot128 + 128 = 73{,}856$ parameters.
- **SeparableConv2D**: depthwise $3\cdot3\cdot64 = 576$, pointwise $64\cdot128 = 8{,}192$, bias $128$: total $8{,}896$.

That is about 8 times fewer parameters, and a similar reduction in multiply-adds per output position. The book (p.302) explains the underlying assumption: spatial locations are highly correlated but channels are fairly independent, so learning spatial and channel-wise features separately loses little.

deeper.title: Shape walk-through of the example network
deeper.body:
Assume a 180×180 RGB input (the size used for cats vs. dogs in chapter 8; the template itself leaves height/width symbolic).

1. Input: (180, 180, 3)
2. SeparableConv2D(32, 3): (178, 178, 32)
3. SeparableConv2D(64, 3): (176, 176, 64)
4. MaxPooling2D(2): (88, 88, 64)
5. SeparableConv2D(64, 3): (86, 86, 64)
6. SeparableConv2D(128, 3): (84, 84, 128)

On p.627 the network continues with another pool, two convolutions and global average pooling, ending in a 128-vector that feeds the Dense head. Notice the trend the book pointed out on p.269: depth grows while spatial size shrinks.

deeper.title: Picking the head: one table for p.625–626
deeper.body:
| Task | Last layer | Loss | Targets |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary classification | `Dense(1, sigmoid)` | `binary_crossentropy` | 0 or 1 |
| Single-label multiclass | `Dense(num_classes, softmax)` | `categorical_crossentropy` / `sparse_categorical_crossentropy` | one-hot / integer |
| Multilabel | `Dense(num_classes, sigmoid)` | `binary_crossentropy` | k-hot |
| Regression | `Dense(num_values)` (no activation) | `mse` | real values |

The body of the network can be anything (MLP, ConvNet, RNN, Transformer); these head/loss pairs stay the same across all the architectures reviewed in this section.

misconceptions.claim: A regression model should end with relu so that outputs stay positive.
misconceptions.correction: The book's template uses no activation. A relu output can get stuck at zero with zero gradient; normalize targets instead, or use a softplus if strict positivity is needed (beyond the book).
The page stresses that the idea works in any dimensionality: Conv1D for sequences, Conv2D for images, Conv3D for volumes.

misconceptions.claim: Max pooling is there only to save computation.
misconceptions.correction: It also lets later convolution layers see a larger part of the input, building the spatial hierarchy of features.

misconceptions.claim: Multilabel classification uses softmax like multiclass classification.
misconceptions.correction: Multilabel uses one sigmoid per class and binary_crossentropy, because labels are not mutually exclusive.

takeaways: Regression: end with Dense(num_values) and no activation; MSE is the default loss.
Multilabel classification: Dense(num_classes, sigmoid) with binary_crossentropy and k-hot targets.
Convolutions share one local transformation across all positions, giving translation invariance and data efficiency.
Use Conv1D/Conv2D/Conv3D according to the number of spatial axes; SeparableConv2D is a leaner alternative to Conv2D.
ConvNets alternate convolution and max pooling, then Flatten or global pooling, then Dense layers.

questions.question: You want to predict both the latitude and longitude of a photo from image features. Which output layer and loss match the book's regression template?
questions.explanation: Regression toward a vector uses one unit per value and no activation, with MSE. Sigmoid/softmax with crossentropy are classification heads; Dense(1) would predict only one value.

questions.question: Why does applying the same transformation to every patch make convolution layers data efficient?
questions.answer: Because a pattern learned at one location is automatically recognized at all other locations (translation invariance via weight sharing), so the model does not need training examples of every pattern at every position, and it has far fewer parameters to fit.
questions.explanation: This is the e07 argument, developed in chapter 8 (p.259): the visual world is translation invariant, so a prior that matches it needs fewer samples.

questions.question: Give two reasons the book gives for using pooling layers in a ConvNet.
questions.answer: To keep feature maps at a reasonable size as the number of features grows, and to let subsequent convolution layers see a greater spatial extent of the input.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in e08. Without downsampling, activations would be huge and top layers would still only see small windows of the original image.

questions.question: Which Keras layer would you use to process 3D medical scans (volumes)?
questions.explanation: The page maps dimensionality to layer: Conv1D for sequences, Conv2D for images, Conv3D for volumes. SeparableConv2D is a 2D layer.

questions.question: In the multilabel template, why is the loss binary_crossentropy even though there are num_classes outputs?
questions.answer: Each output unit is an independent binary (present/absent) decision with its own sigmoid, so binary crossentropy is applied per unit and averaged.
questions.explanation: Labels are not mutually exclusive in multilabel problems, so each class is its own Bernoulli variable; categorical crossentropy would assume exactly one correct class.

questions.question: What is the difference between ending a ConvNet with Flatten and ending it with a global pooling layer?
questions.answer: Flatten keeps every spatial position as a separate feature (large vector, many Dense parameters, position-specific); global pooling reduces each channel to one number (vector of length channels), which is compact and position-independent.
questions.explanation: The page names both options for turning feature maps into vectors. The p.627 example and chapter 8 (p.269) use GlobalAveragePooling2D.

questions.question: Without looking, write the four lines that turn a hidden representation x into a compiled regression model with three continuous outputs.
questions.answer: outputs = layers.Dense(3)(x); model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs); model.compile(optimizer="rmsprop", loss="mse") — with no activation on the output layer.
questions.explanation: Compare with the regression code block on this page; the key detail is the missing activation argument.
